DNA extraction, microsatellite amplification, and genotyping: We extracted DNA from fecal samples using the First-DNA all tissue kit (Genial®). We characterized genetic variation in Guinea baboons by assessing the individual allele variation on 24 polymorphic autosomal microsatellite markers (see Table 1). This microsatellite panel was developed based on microsatellite markers used in humans and reported to also amplify in baboons (Roeder et al., 2009; Rogers et al., 2000), which have been successfully multiplexed in several studies of Guinea baboons (Kopp et al., 2015; Ferreira da Silva et al., 2014, 2018) including our study population (Patzelt et al, 2014). Note that the current panel (described in Table 1) was modified compared to the initial panel used by Patzelt et al. (2014). The 24 markers were amplified in 5 different multiplex systems (mean number of loci per multiplex, 4.80 ± 1.10 SD) using the Multiplex PCR Kit (QIAGEN) and fluorescent-labelled primers in concentrations ranging from 0.05 to 0.5 µM. PCR cycling conditions included a hot start polymerase activation step at 95°C for 15min, followed by 40 cycles with denaturation at 94°C for 30s, primer annealing at 57°C for 40s, elongation at 72°C for 40s, and a single final elongation step at 72°C for 30min. Detailed information regarding loci identities, primer sequences and concentrations, and fluorescent dyes are reported in table 1. PCR products were separated and detected through capillary gel electrophoresis on an ABI 3130xL Genetic Analyzer (16 capillary sequencer, Applied Biosystems®, USA). Microsatellite allele sizes were evaluated in comparison with the GeneScanTM -400HD size standard using Gene Mapper 5 (Applied Biosystems®). Allele calling for each locus was repeated until 5 completely consistent calls were achieved. To avoid contamination, extraction, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and fragment length analysis were performed in separate rooms and monitored with negative controls. steps.title: Collect fecal samples
steps.instruction: Immediately after defecation, identify the individual, collect approximately 5 g of fecal material from the surface of the bolus, and place it into a sterile tube pre‑filled with 90 % ethanol.

substeps.instruction: Identify the individual that produced the fresh feces.
Using a clean tool, scoop ~5 g of material from the surface of the bolus.
Transfer the material into a sterile tube containing 90 % ethanol.

steps.title: Preserve and store samples
steps.instruction: Apply a two‑step preservation: keep the ethanol‑submerged sample, then desiccate with silica beads, ship yearly to the German Primate Center, and store at –20 °C.

substeps.instruction: Leave the tube in 90 % ethanol for initial conservation.
After ethanol preservation, add silica beads to desiccate the sample.
Ship the preserved samples to the German Primate Center once per year.
Upon receipt, store all samples at –20 °C.

steps.title: Calculate marker statistics and filter loci
steps.instruction: Using the genotype data for all 24 microsatellite markers, compute descriptive statistics, test for Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium and null alleles, and discard any loci that fail these checks.

substeps.instruction: With R package PopGenReport, calculate for each of the 24 markers: F_IS, expected heterozygosity, observed heterozygosity, and perform a Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium test.
Run MICRO‑CHECKER to detect the presence of null alleles at each locus.
Exclude any locus that shows evidence of null alleles or a statistically significant deviation from Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium from all subsequent analyses.

steps.title: Simulate relatedness estimators
steps.instruction: Determine the most accurate relatedness estimator by simulating known relationships and comparing estimator performance with Spearman correlation.

substeps.instruction: Load the R package “related”.
Simulate 100 pairs of individuals for each of the four known relatedness categories: parent‑offspring, full‑sibling, half‑sibling, and unrelated.

For each of the seven estimators (five non‑likelihood: Queller‑Goodnight, Li, Ritland, Lynch‑Ritland, Wang 2002; two likelihood: Milligan, Wang 2007), calculate relatedness values for the simulated pairs.
Compute Spearman’s rank correlation between the simulated (expected) and calculated (observed) relatedness values for each estimator.
Select the estimator with the highest Spearman correlation coefficient for use with the empirical dataset.

steps.title: Estimate pairwise relatedness
steps.instruction: Apply the chosen estimator to the genotype dataset to obtain dyadic relatedness values and interpret them according to the estimator’s scale.

substeps.instruction: Run the selected estimator on all individual genotype pairs to generate relatedness coefficients.

Interpret the coefficients: for the two maximum‑likelihood estimators the range is 0 to 1; for the five non‑likelihood estimators the range is –1 to 1, where negative values indicate below‑average relatedness.

steps.title: Perform parentage analysis with Cervus
steps.instruction: Assign paternity using Cervus by first simulating parentage, then running maternity checks and trio likelihood paternity analyses with strict confidence criteria.

substeps.instruction: In Cervus, run a simulated parentage analysis with 10 000 offspring using the following parameters: proportion of potential sires sampled = 0.95, proportion of typed loci = 1.00, proportion of mistyped loci = 0.01, confidence thresholds = 95 % (strict) and 80 % (relaxed).
Include all females from the study groups; examine any documented transfers of mothers to another primary male’s unit between conception and birth.
Perform a maternity likelihood analysis for all mother‑offspring pairs, accepting only candidate mothers with 0 mismatched alleles.
Run a trio‑likelihood paternity analysis using the known mother for each offspring to identify the most likely father.
For offspring where the mother is unknown or the field‑observed mother does not match the genetic data, repeat the paternity analysis without a mother genotype.
Include all adolescent (large juvenile and subadult) and adult males as potential sires.
Assign paternity when a male is the most likely father, has 0 to a maximum of 1 mismatched allele, and the assignment confidence exceeds 95 % (strict criterion).
